name: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM)

lead: MSM is a sulfur compound found in trace amounts in foods and sold as a supplement for joints, skin, hair and nails. People take it for smoother, healthier-looking skin, better hair and nails, and joints that stay comfortable for training.

The idea is that it supplies sulfur to skin and hair tissue. Small randomised trials of skin and hair outcomes report improved wrinkles and hydration, though they are small and short. Forum claims about lightening skin or eye colour and preserving height appear only in anecdote.

paras: Taken orally as a daily powder or capsule, and also used in topical products. Users commonly combine it with collagen, vitamin C or joint supplements and judge results over several weeks.
Animal studies suggest very low toxicity, and a branded form received an FDA non-objection letter for GRAS status. It has no approved medical uses, and long-term human data are limited.

chain: Sulfur supplied to skin and hair
angle.text: MSM is taken for softer skin, stronger hair and nails, and comfortable joints for training, on the idea that it supplies sulfur to those tissues. A few small skin trials exist; the claims about lightening skin or eyes and preserving height rest on anecdote.

lead: Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM, dimethyl sulfone) is a small organic sulfur compound, (CH3)2SO2, that occurs in trace amounts in some plants and foods and is detectable in human blood. It is sold as an inexpensive oral supplement, in tablet or powder form, and appears in topical skin products. [1][2]

People take it for appearance in three main ways: for skin firmness, wrinkles and hydration; for hair and nail quality; and, through a longer chain, for joint and muscle comfort that keeps training and daily movement going. Small randomised trials of skin, hair and nail outcomes have been published, while the larger body of human research concerns knee osteoarthritis, exercise recovery and seasonal allergy symptoms. [2][3]

The US FDA has not approved MSM for any medical use, though a manufacturer's 2007 notification that a branded form is generally recognised as safe (GRAS) received a no-objection letter in 2008. [2] Wikipedia describes the evidence for most claims as weak, and a 2008 systematic review of knee osteoarthritis trials concluded that no definitive conclusion could be drawn. [2] A 2017 review in Nutrients, by contrast, summarised animal and human work as showing improvements in inflammation, joint and muscle pain and oxidative-stress measures. [3]
On looksmax.org it is discussed for skin softness and tone, hair texture and joint comfort, with claims about skin or eye lightening that the thread's own author describes as anecdotal. [4]
infobox: Trace amounts in many foods; found in human blood and cerebrospinal fluid [2]

paras: MSM is a white crystalline solid, soluble in water and chemically fairly inert. It is the simplest sulfone and is formed by oxidation of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO); in the environment it is an intermediate in the oxidation of dimethyl sulfide. [2] It occurs in trace amounts in some primitive plants and in small amounts in many foods and beverages. [2]

In humans it is thought to come from diet, gut bacteria and the body's own methanethiol metabolism, and it has been detected in blood and cerebrospinal fluid. [2] Wikipedia notes that no Dietary Reference Intake or Daily Value exists for sulfur, and lists cruciferous vegetables, garlic, onions, legumes, nuts, seeds, milk and eggs among sulfur-containing foods. [2] Reviews of sulfur in nutrition describe the sulfur-containing amino acids as the main dietary route for the element, which frames the argument supplement makers make for MSM. [5]

Supplement makers promote MSM for skin firmness, wrinkles, hair and nails, and for a general anti-ageing effect. [2] A 2015 randomised trial in 20 women, led by Anthonavage and colleagues, reported fewer and less severe facial wrinkles and better firmness, tone and texture on a daily oral dose of 3 g. [2] A later study by Muizzuddin and Benjamin enrolled 20 participants at two dose levels and reported improved wrinkles, firmness and hydration; a companion analysis from the same work reported better hair shine, volume and appearance and better nail shine and appearance. [2]

A 2019 Italian placebo-controlled trial by Guaitolini and colleagues tested a combination of MSM, hyaluronic acid and L-carnosine and reported better facial hydration and elasticity and reduced sebaceous secretion. [2] Because that product combined three ingredients, its results cannot be assigned to MSM alone. [2]

Topical MSM products are also sold. Wikipedia notes that, as with its relative DMSO, MSM may act in a topical formula partly as a skin-permeation enhancer, which would be separate from any direct effect of its own. [2]

MSM is most often sold for joint pain. People who train hard describe joint comfort as a way of keeping a routine going, and consistent training is the route to a more muscular physique; this is the link the looksmaxxing discussion draws between a joint supplement and appearance. [4] Small exercise trials are summarised below.
Other uses reported in the research literature include seasonal allergic rhinitis, immune function after exhaustive exercise and lipid profile, discussed under Clinical studies. [2][6]

Orally taken MSM is absorbed and crosses the blood-brain barrier. A 2001 magnetic resonance spectroscopy study detected MSM in the brains of seven people who took it at 1 to 3 g daily (four patients with memory loss and three healthy volunteers); it was not detected in 25 drug-naive volunteers or in hundreds of other patients scanned over the preceding decade, and the authors observed no adverse clinical or neurochemical effects. [7] Supplement use therefore adds to a baseline that comes from diet, gut bacteria and metabolism. [2]

The mechanism behind any appearance or comfort outcome has not been established. [2] Laboratory work reports anti-inflammatory activity: a 2015 cell study found that MSM attenuated NLRP3 inflammasome activation in mouse and human macrophages and reduced expression of several inflammatory signalling molecules, with DMSO showing a comparable effect. [8] The 2017 Nutrients review describes antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions as the basis for its common use. [3]

The sulfur-supplementation argument holds that supplying more sulfur could support sulfur-rich tissues such as skin, hair, nails and connective tissue. Wikipedia traces this claim to Robert Herschler's work. [2]

The skin studies are small (about 20 participants), short and in some cases involve combination products. [2] The knee osteoarthritis trials are more numerous and have mixed results, summarised below. A large 2018 network meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, covering 69 randomised trials of 20 oral supplements, placed MSM in a group that showed statistically significant pain improvements of unclear clinical importance. [9]

Proponents point to the consistency of reported tolerability and to positive pain trials, while reviewers point to small samples, industry links in several trials and methodological problems in the older knee studies. [2][3]

Small human trials suggest MSM may reduce markers of exercise-induced muscle damage and raise antioxidant capacity, according to Wikipedia's summary, and one randomised trial of exhaustive exercise reported that people on MSM kept a stronger immune response afterwards than the placebo group. [2] The reasoning for appearance is indirect: less soreness could mean more consistent training. The trials are small and the findings have not been replicated at scale. [2]

Animal research indicates very low oral and topical toxicity, and the Natural Medicines database rates MSM "possibly safe" at therapeutic doses. [2] The 2017 review describes it as well tolerated by most people at up to 4 g daily with few and mild side effects. [3] A 2019 safety analysis of a 16-week randomised low back pain trial in a military family medicine clinic found no difference from placebo in blood counts, liver enzymes, creatinine, weight or blood pressure at 6 g daily. [10]

A nematode study reported dose-dependent decreases in lifespan and fertility in a mutant strain; its relevance to humans is unknown. [2] MSM has also been reported as a cutting agent in illicit methamphetamine. [2] Long-term human data beyond several months are limited. [3][10]

MSM has no approved medical use in the US. A manufacturer notified the FDA of GRAS status for a branded MSM in 2007, and the FDA's February 2008 response was a letter of no objection (GRN 000229), which permits use in processed foods; GRAS addresses safety, not efficacy. [2] As a dietary supplement it is sold without a prescription in many markets, with marketing claims about skin, joints and immune health. [2]

MSM became known to biochemists as a metabolite of DMSO, a sulfur-containing solvent; a 1975 paper by Kocsis and colleagues proposed that some of DMSO's biological effects may be mediated by MSM. [2] Biochemist Robert Herschler filed a patent for MSM as a dietary supplement in 1982, and US 4,514,421 was issued on 30 April 1985. [2]

Early human reports of the 2000s included a pilot knee osteoarthritis trial (2006) and a multicentre open-label allergy study. [2][11] A manufacturer's GRAS notification in 2007 and the FDA's no-objection letter in 2008 followed, and the first published study of MSM for skin health appeared in 2015. [2] Popular alternative-medicine books such as The Miracle of MSM (1999) helped spread the supplement beyond the research literature. [2]

Wikipedia describes supplement marketing that cites anti-inflammatory, skin, ageing and immune benefits, while noting that evidence for most claims is limited. [2] MSM is also used as a high-temperature industrial solvent in molten form. [2] Because it is a cheap, simple compound sold in bulk powder and tablets, price comparison is a recurring theme in forum threads. [4]

A looksmax.org informational thread describes MSM as a sulfur compound for joints, skin softening and lightening, and hair strength, and the original poster states that the information is largely anecdotal because research on eye or skin colour is sparse, adding that the supplement "doesn't really have any sides". [4] The thread says some people argue that very high intake lightened their eye colour, particularly with a light-eyed parent, and that others report slightly looser curls. [4]

Replies are mixed: one user reports no confirmation of the skin or eye claims after five years but continues to use it for spinal joint comfort and for holding morning height through the day, and another uses it for ankle and wrist discomfort. [4] The height-maintenance idea rests on the broader belief that spinal disc and joint health affect how much height is lost over a day, which these threads discuss without published MSM-specific measurements. [4]

The published skin work is the 2015 trial of 20 women (3 g daily, fewer and less severe wrinkles with better firmness, tone and texture), the Muizzuddin and Benjamin study of 20 participants at two doses (improved wrinkles, firmness and hydration, with hair and nail appearance outcomes reported separately), and the 2019 combination-supplement trial (hydration, elasticity, less sebum). [2]

A 2006 pilot randomised, double-blind trial in 50 adults aged 40 to 76 with knee osteoarthritis gave 3 g of MSM or placebo twice daily for 12 weeks. MSM produced significant decreases in WOMAC pain and physical function impairment and improved activities of daily living on the SF-36, with no change in stiffness or total symptom scores; the authors called it a pilot and said long-term benefits and safety could not be confirmed. [11]

A 2004 randomised trial of 118 people with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis compared glucosamine, MSM, their combination and placebo over 12 weeks and reported that all three active arms improved pain and swelling indices compared with placebo, with the combination showing the largest changes. [12] A 2023 randomised trial in 88 healthy Japanese adults with mild knee pain reported a significantly better total Japanese Knee Osteoarthritis Measure score after 12 weeks on MSM (p = 0.046). [13]

Not every trial was positive. In a 2017 randomised trial of 180 military initial entry trainees aged 18 to 40, 3 g daily for eight weeks did not significantly improve any KOOS or mood subscale at 30 or 60 days, although the authors judged it safe. [14] The 2008 systematic review of osteoarthritis trials reported methodological problems and no definitive conclusion. [2] Registered trials include knee osteoarthritis studies, a 100-participant phase 3 trial in low back pain, a trial on knee laxity in 32 people, and a study of aromatase-inhibitor joint pain. [15][16][17][18][19]

In a 2021 randomised, double-blind trial, 22 overweight or obese adults completed 16 weeks of daily MSM or placebo; HDL cholesterol was higher than baseline at 8 and 16 weeks in the MSM group, while other outcomes including body composition were also measured. [6] A registered cardiometabolic study in obesity enrolled 43 people. [20] A small phase 2 allergen-challenge study enrolled 15 people, and a randomised trial of seasonal allergic rhinitis compared three daily amounts, with the middle amount performing best on symptom scores. [2][21] Most registered studies do not post summarised results.

lore.intro: Looksmaxxing forums discuss MSM mainly for skin softness and tone, hair texture and joint health, often with the caveat, voiced by the thread's own author, that the evidence is anecdotal. [4]

timeline.event: Kocsis and colleagues publish on DMSO metabolites; MSM is proposed as a mediator of some DMSO effects. [2]
Robert Herschler files a patent for MSM as a dietary supplement (US 4,514,421, issued 30 April 1985). [2]
Popular book The Miracle of MSM is published, an example of alternative-medicine promotion. [2]
MRS study detects MSM in the human brain after oral intake. [7]
Randomised trial compares glucosamine, MSM and their combination in knee osteoarthritis. [12]
Pilot randomised trial reports lower knee osteoarthritis pain and better function with MSM. [11]
GRAS notification and FDA no-objection letter for a branded MSM. [2]
Systematic review finds methodological problems and no definitive conclusion in knee osteoarthritis trials. [2]
First published skin-health study of MSM; NLRP3 inflammasome cell study published. [2][8]
Nutrients review on applications and safety; military knee-pain prevention trial reports no significant improvement. [3][14]
Network meta-analysis of oral supplements for osteoarthritis includes MSM. [9]
Randomised trial in overweight adults reports higher HDL cholesterol on MSM. [6]
Japanese randomised trial reports better knee quality-of-life scores in people with mild knee pain. [13]
